title: How to Make Cannabutter: Step-by-Step Guide
h1: How to Make Cannabutter at Home, and Dose It Safely
metaDescription: How to make cannabutter at home: choosing flower and butter, decarbing, stovetop or slow-cooker infusion, potency per tablespoon, cooking and storage.
excerpt: A home cannabutter guide covering the steps people often get wrong: decarbing first, keeping the heat low, estimating strength per tablespoon and storing it safely.
keyTakeaways: THC dissolves in fat, not water, so butter carries it into whatever you bake or cook.
Decarb first: baking the flower for 30 to 45 minutes around 240°F turns THCA into THC more reliably than a gentle steep, which converts it slowly.
Keep the infusion below a simmer (160 to 200°F) for two to three hours.
Grams × 1,000 × THC% gives the most THC your batch can hold; real batches come in lower and vary.
Try a small portion, wait at least 2 hours, and label and store your butter where kids and pets can't reach it.
body:
Learning how to make cannabutter comes down to three stages: decarb your cannabis in a low oven, steep it gently in butter for a few hours, then strain out the plant material. Most batches go wrong in one of three ways: the decarb gets skipped, the heat climbs too high or the strength is a guess. This guide walks through each stage, a simple recipe, the math for estimating THC per tablespoon, and how to cook with, store and label what you make.

## What cannabutter is, and why fat carries THC

Cannabutter is butter infused with cannabis. It works because THC barely dissolves in water but mixes readily into fats and oils. During a long, gentle steep, the butterfat pulls cannabinoids out of the plant. Once infused, the butter carries THC into anything you bake or cook with it, which is exactly why measuring matters.

## Choosing your cannabis: flower, trim or shake

Butter doesn't need top-shelf buds. Smaller buds and shake work well, since you're extracting cannabinoids rather than smoking the flower; our guide to [buds, shake and popcorn nugs](/blog/cannabis-bud-vs-shake-vs-popcorn/) explains the differences. Trim, the small leaves cut away from the buds, carries less resin, so the same weight makes milder butter.

Two numbers matter most:

- **THC percentage.** Note it from the label so you can estimate strength later.
- **Quantity.** For a first batch, about 3.5 grams per cup of butter keeps things manageable. You can always go stronger next time.

Pick up flower from [your store's online menu](/shop/), and ask our budtenders about THC levels and value options.

## Choosing your butter: salted, unsalted, clarified or ghee

- **Unsalted butter** leaves the seasoning up to you, which helps in baking.
- **Salted butter** is fine for savory cooking.
- **Clarified butter or ghee** has had its milk solids removed, so it's less likely to scorch at the same heat.

Regular butter holds water and milk solids along with its fat. Adding a cup of water to the pot keeps the temperature from creeping too high, and the water separates out once the butter chills.

## Step one: decarboxylation

Raw flower is mostly THCA, which needs heat to turn into THC. Can you skip this step? You can, but expect weaker, less predictable butter. In lab tests on cannabis extracts, conversion still wasn't complete after an hour at temperatures under about 212°F (100°C), the range a butter infusion stays in. At 230°F (110°C), THCA had nearly disappeared within about 30 minutes.

At home, break the flower into small pieces, spread it on a parchment-lined tray and bake it for 30 to 45 minutes at about 240°F, until it looks golden and dry. Our [decarboxylation guide](/blog/cannabis-decarboxylation/) covers the details and other methods.

## Methods compared: stovetop, slow cooker, double boiler and infuser

| Method | Setup | Best when | Keep in mind |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stovetop with water | Butter, water and decarbed flower on the lowest burner setting | You want simple, with no special gear | Stir often, and don't let the water cook off |
| Slow cooker | The same mix on low, lid on | You'd like to walk away for a while | Some cookers run hot, so check with a thermometer |
| Double boiler | A bowl set over barely simmering water | You want gentle, even heat | Top up the water as it evaporates |
| Countertop infuser | An appliance that heats and stirs at a set temperature | You want low effort and less smell | It costs more; follow the maker's directions |

Whichever you choose, keep the mixture between about 160 and 200°F, steaming but never boiling, for two to three hours.

## How to make cannabutter: the recipe at a glance

The recipe card below lists the ingredients and steps. Before you start, gather a baking sheet, parchment, a saucepan or slow cooker, cheesecloth or a fine-mesh strainer, a heat-safe bowl and a kitchen thermometer.

## Dosing and safety: estimating mg per tablespoon

Homemade butter varies, so read every number as a ceiling and an estimate. Here's the math:

1. **THC in your flower:** take the weight in grams, times 1,000, times the THC percentage (20% becomes 0.20). For 3.5 grams at 20% THC: 3.5 × 1,000 × 0.20 = 700 mg.
2. **Per tablespoon:** a cup of butter holds 16 tablespoons, so 700 ÷ 16 ≈ 44 mg per tablespoon at most.
3. **Per teaspoon:** a tablespoon is 3 teaspoons, so about 15 mg per teaspoon at most.

Real numbers come in lower. Some THC is lost to heat, some stays in the strained plant material, and butter doesn't always mix evenly. For scale, Michigan won't let a licensed adult-use edible exceed 10 mg of THC in a single serving. If a recipe uses 4 tablespoons of this butter across 16 brownies, each one holds about 11 mg at most; swap plain butter in for part of it to go milder.

Test a quarter or half portion first, then give it at least two hours, because an edible can be that slow to show its effects. Only serve infused food to adults 21 and older who know exactly what they're eating. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) explains starting amounts in more detail.

## Cooking with it: baking, savory dishes and spreads

- **Baking:** use cannabutter for some or all of the butter in brownies, cookies or bars, and mix the batter thoroughly so it spreads evenly.
- **Savory dishes:** stir a measured pat into pasta, rice or vegetables off the heat. Long, high heat can break THC down, so add it at the end.
- **Spreads:** measured cannabutter on toast or a warm biscuit is easy to portion.

Measure with spoons every time. For dressings and sautés, [canna oil](/blog/canna-oil/) can be easier to work with.

## Storage and labeling

- **Label it.** Write what it is, the date and your estimated mg per tablespoon on the container.
- **Fridge:** keep it sealed and use it within 4 days, the limit the CDC sets for homemade oils made with herbs; we apply the same caution to infused butter.
- **Freezer:** freeze small portions for longer storage. Food held at a constant 0°F is always safe to eat, though its quality fades over time.
- **Keep it in your kitchen.** Michigan's law allows adults to give cannabis to another adult 21 or older, but only as a true gift, with nothing given back in exchange. Homemade butter, and anything baked with it, isn't for selling or trading.
- **Out of reach:** store it where kids and pets can't get to it, and never next to your regular butter.

That last point matters. U.S. poison centers logged 207 edible cannabis exposures in children younger than 6 in 2017. By 2021 the yearly count had reached 3,054, and almost all of those exposures happened at home. For pets, see our [guide to cannabis and pet safety](/blog/cannabis-and-pets-safety-guide/).

21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: How long does it take to make cannabutter?
faq.a: Budget three to four hours, most of it hands-off: 30 to 45 minutes to decarb, two to three hours of gentle infusion and a few minutes to strain. With the water method, add a few hours in the fridge so the butter can firm up and separate from the water before you lift it off.

faq.q: How much cannabis do I need for a stick of butter?
faq.a: It depends on your flower's THC and how strong you want the butter. As a starting point, about 1.75 grams of 20% THC flower per stick works out to at most about 44 mg of THC per tablespoon, since a stick is 8 tablespoons. Use less for milder butter, and run the math with your own flower's numbers.

The usual culprits are a skipped decarb, flower with less THC than you thought, or heat that ran too high. Uneven mixing can also leave one brownie strong and the next mild. And give it time: an edible may need up to two hours before you notice it, so it may simply be too soon to judge.

Sealed in the fridge, use it within 4 days, the CDC's limit for homemade oils made with herbs, which we apply to infused butter too. For longer storage, freeze it in small, labeled portions; food held at a constant 0°F stays safe, though flavor slowly fades. Throw out any butter that smells sour or shows mold, and keep every container clearly marked.

faq.q: Can I make cannabutter without decarbing?
faq.a: You can, but expect weaker and less predictable butter. Raw flower is mostly THCA, and a low-temperature steep converts it slowly; in lab tests on extracts, conversion wasn't finished after an hour below about 212°F. A 30- to 45-minute bake at around 240°F before infusing is the more reliable route.

ingredients: 3.5 grams (an eighth) of cannabis flower, broken into small pieces
steps: Preheat the oven to 240°F. Lay the flower pieces out on a baking sheet lined with parchment and bake for 30 to 45 minutes, until golden and dry, then let them cool.
Melt the butter with the water in a saucepan on your burner's lowest setting.
Stir in the decarbed flower. Keep the pot steaming but never boiling, about 160 to 200°F, for 2 to 3 hours, stirring occasionally and adding a splash of water if the level drops.
Line a fine-mesh strainer with cheesecloth, set it over a heat-safe bowl and pour the mixture through. Press lightly; hard squeezing pushes more plant flavor into the butter.
Chill the bowl for a few hours, until the butter firms into a solid layer above the water.
Lift the butter off, blot any water from the underside and discard the water. Pack the butter into a sealed container, label it and store it in the fridge or freezer.
recipe.dosingNote: This is an estimate, not a promise. Using 3.5 g of flower that tests at 20% THC: 3.5 × 1,000 × 0.20 = 700 mg of THC at most, or about 44 mg per tablespoon across the batch's 16 tablespoons. The real figure depends on your flower's actual potency and on how much THC the decarb and the infusion lose, so expect less, spread unevenly. Start low with a quarter teaspoon (about 4 mg at most), and let at least 2 hours pass before you decide on more. Label the butter and everything you make with it, and keep all of it away from children and pets.

claims.claim: In lab tests on extracts, conversion wasn't complete after an hour below about 212°F (100°C); at 230°F (110°C) THCA nearly disappeared within about 30 minutes (body and FAQ)
claims.source: Wang 2016: 'At temperatures lower than 100°C, the reaction did not reach completion within 60 min. At higher temperatures, the concentration of THCA-A approached zero in 30, 9, and 6 min at 110°C, 130°C, and 145°C'

claims.claim: Takeaway: a gentle steep 'can't finish' the THCA-to-THC conversion on its own
claims.fix: Changed to 'more reliably than a gentle steep, which converts it slowly'. Wang's THCA rate constants (0.18 x 10^-3 /s at 80°C, 0.66 x 10^-3 /s at 95°C, extracts) imply a 2-3 hour steep near 200°F converts most THCA, while one near 160°F converts roughly half; the study only measured 60 minutes
claims.source: Wang 2016, Table 2 (rate constants) and first-order kinetics stated in the abstract

claims.claim: Home decarb: 30 to 45 minutes at about 240°F, until golden and dry
claims.source: Practice consistent with Wang 2016 (110°C/230°F about 30 min in extracts); presented as a home method, not a lab result

claims.claim: Infuse at about 160 to 200°F, steaming but never boiling, for two to three hours
claims.source: Practice; stays below the 212°F boiling point; no potency promise attached

claims.claim: Potency math: 3.5 g x 1,000 x 0.20 = 700 mg; about 44 mg per tablespoon (16 per cup); about 15 mg per teaspoon; about 11 mg per brownie (4 tbsp across 16); about 4 mg per quarter teaspoon; 1.75 g per stick gives about 44 mg per tablespoon (8 per stick)
Real batches come in lower: heat losses, THC left in the strained plant, uneven mixing

review.notes: Fact-check 2026-10-24: 22 claims checked, 1 fixed (overstated takeaway on what a steep can convert, checked against Wang 2016's rate constants). All dosing arithmetic re-done. Writer's notes: no potency promises (ceilings only), no brand-name infusers, no high-heat method. Selling rules beyond the gifting claim are not in facts/law-facts.json, so 'not for selling or trading' rests on the gifting condition only. Cross-batch sweep 2026-10-24 (orchestrator, after the fact-check workflow): Aligned with canna-butter-recipe, canna-oil and canna-oil-recipe: the CDC's 4-day fridge limit for homemade oils made with garlic or herbs (CDC Botulism Prevention, opened by the batch 26 checker 2026-10-24), applied to infused butter as canna-butter-recipe does. The earlier 'about two weeks' was an unsourced quality estimate. CDC Botulism Prevention added to sources.
